messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Self-Consciousness: Being seen, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Mehta was a 41-year-old South Asian park ranger who had been in a steady relationship for several years and, until recently, had prided himself on being calm, practical, and hard to rattle. That changed after a period of captivity overseas, an experience he still described only in fragments because the full account felt too shameful and too close. What stayed with him were not stories in sequence but a set of snapshots: a metal door half open, the glare of a fluorescent light, a boot stepping into view, the hard grip on his arm, and the taste of fear in his mouth. When those images came back, they did so as if they were happening in the room with him; at times he could feel the old ache and pressure in the same parts of his body, and at other times he could describe the scene with a flat, numbed distance, as though it had happened to someone else. Even in the early weeks after he returned home, unexpected movement nearby made him flinch as though he were back in danger, and he could not trust reassurance. Friends told him he was safe; his partner said the doors were locked; Arjun still scanned the room, convinced that safety could be taken away without warning. He also began to feel permanently humiliated by what had happened, certain that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, and the humiliation deepened his sense that he was set apart from everyone around him.

Those appraisals quickly shaped how he moved through the world. Arjun came to believe that being seen carried risk, so he made himself smaller in public, avoided eye contact, and went along with whatever others wanted because agreeing felt safer than being noticed. He also imposed strict control over what he ate, cutting portions and skipping meals because regulating food gave him one area where he could feel disciplined and not at the mercy of anyone else. At the same time, he found himself replaying scenes of revenge against the people responsible, imagining power reversed and himself no longer trapped. Yet these efforts never settled him for long. The more he tried to control his eating, please others, or mentally punish his captors, the more the images returned in sharper pieces, each flash of the event seeming to confirm how isolated and humiliated he had become. The memory was especially liable to be pulled loose by military topics; if someone at home mentioned the army, or if a news report showed uniforms, his mind jumped straight back to those few terrible moments. Uniforms also set off the same reaction at work, where, as a park ranger, he sometimes encountered law enforcement or search-and-rescue personnel in similar clothing. Being seen in those moments felt exposing, and once he was self-conscious under someone’s gaze, he would think again that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate, which only made the old images more vivid and shameful.

As the months passed, the memory itself started to drive the rest of the cycle. A sudden return of the snapshot images could bring a wave of bodily pain and make him feel as if the captivity were happening again, and once that threat feeling rose he became even more certain that he could not trust safety. When he was jolted by a sound or an abrupt movement on a trail, the room or forest seemed to tilt toward the past, and that sense of danger made the fragments of memory sharper still. The memories, in turn, fed back into his negative beliefs: each return seemed to prove that he remained isolated, permanently humiliated, and somehow at fault. Because he felt that way, he redoubled his efforts to keep control, eating even more strictly, deferring to others, and fantasizing about revenge in private. But these strategies brought their own costs. Skipping meals left him shaky and more reactive to sudden movement, which made the world feel even less safe. Going along with everyone else left him resentful and more aware of being unseen. Revenge fantasies kept his mind circling the captivity long after work, making the images easier to summon and the humiliation harder to shake. And once he was already keyed up, even a uniform at the trailhead, a military comment on television, or a stranger turning too quickly on the path could trigger the same surge of dread and pull him back into the snapshots again.

By the time he sought help, Arjun was still functioning at work but only by keeping himself tightly managed and on edge. His partner had noticed that he was distant at home, jumpy when someone moved unexpectedly, and increasingly unwilling to go out unless he could control the setting. What finally brought him in was the fear that he was becoming trapped in the same private loop every day: the images, the humiliation, the rigid control, the constant scanning. He said he was most afraid that the captivity had permanently changed him, but he was also hoping that therapy might help him feel safe enough to stop living as if danger were always one step away.
